Vomiting without a fever in babies and children: causes and when to get help

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A baby or child can vomit without having a fever. The cause may be a feeding issue, reflux or a short-lived infection, but a normal temperature does not rule out a serious problem. Age, alertness, hydration, pain and the colour and force of the vomit are more useful than temperature alone. This guide explains the possibilities and the signs that should take priority over home care.

Check for urgent warning signs first

Seek emergency assessment for green vomit, blood or coffee-ground material in vomit, a swollen or very painful abdomen, severe episodes of pain, or a child who is difficult to wake, floppy, confused or struggling to breathe. Green bile can indicate an intestinal blockage. Do not wait for a fever to develop.

Vomiting with a seizure, a severe headache, a recent significant head injury or possible poisoning also needs urgent help. Call emergency services if the child is seriously unwell. If poisoning is possible, contact your local poison service and do not try to make the child vomit.

Get prompt medical advice for repeated or forceful vomiting in a young baby, refusal to feed, inability to keep fluids down, fewer wet diapers, worsening pain or poor weight gain. New repeated vomiting in a baby under three months deserves particular caution, even with a normal temperature.

The following explanations can help you describe what is happening, but they are not a way to exclude an emergency at home. If a child’s condition is deteriorating, act on that change rather than waiting for a set number of hours.

Spit-up, curdled milk and vomiting are different

Spit-up is usually a small, relatively effortless return of milk, sometimes during a burp or shortly after feeding. A baby may remain comfortable and continue growing normally. This is common during infancy, when the mechanism keeping stomach contents down is still developing.

Vomiting usually involves more forceful contraction and may be preceded by retching, gagging, coughing or distress. However, appearance alone is not always clear, especially when the baby has only been drinking milk. A large-looking patch on clothing does not reliably measure how much was brought up.

Milk may look curdled after mixing with stomach acid. That does not mean it fermented, spoiled inside the stomach or was necessarily caused by a disease. Equally, milky or curdled vomit is not automatically harmless if it is repeatedly forceful or the baby looks unwell.

Notice whether the episode was effortless or forceful, its colour, when it happened relative to a feed and how the baby behaved afterwards. A cloth may help with cleanup, but checking breathing and responsiveness matters more than protecting clothes. Persistent vomiting should not be dismissed as ordinary spit-up.

1. Feeding volume, pace or technique

A large feed, a fast bottle flow or difficulty coordinating feeding may contribute to bringing milk back up. These problems can occur while a family is establishing feeding, but it is misleading to say that babies simply need to learn to digest milk or that vomiting after feeds should end at one month.

A feeding review can assess attachment, bottle technique, milk transfer and whether the amount offered suits the baby. With bottle-feeding, respond to pauses and fullness cues instead of encouraging the baby to finish a fixed amount. Burping during natural pauses may improve comfort.

Smaller, more frequent feeds are sometimes suggested, but total nutrition and growth still matter. Do not repeatedly restrict feeds or change formula concentration to control vomiting. Get help if episodes are frequent, increasingly forceful, distressing or associated with fewer wet diapers or poor weight gain.

2. Gastroenteritis, sometimes called a stomach bug

An infection of the stomach and intestines can begin with vomiting before diarrhea appears. It may also cause cramps, reduced appetite and irritability. A fever may be present or absent. The nickname stomach flu does not mean that the illness is caused by the influenza virus.

Many cases are viral and settle with supportive care, but vomiting without diarrhea has other possible causes that need consideration. There is no dependable twenty-four-hour cycle in which vomiting must stop and return, and no rule that fever is absent in young babies.

Vomiting from a typical stomach bug often improves over the next few days, while diarrhea can last longer. The immediate concern is replacing fluid losses and recognising a child who is becoming dehydrated. A very young baby or a child unable to drink should be assessed earlier rather than waiting for an expected illness duration.

Wash hands carefully after diaper changes or cleaning vomit, and clean contaminated surfaces. Antibiotics do not treat an ordinary viral stomach bug. A clinician can decide whether testing or other treatment is needed when symptoms or the history suggest something different.

3. Infant reflux

Reflux happens when stomach contents move back into the food pipe. The muscle at the lower end of the food pipe may allow milk back up more easily in early infancy. Many babies who bring up a little milk are comfortable, feed well and gain weight, and the problem improves as they grow.

Ask for a feeding assessment if the baby seems uncomfortable. Holding the baby upright during a feed and afterwards while you are awake, allowing pauses and avoiding overfeeding may help. Repeated distress, feeding refusal or poor growth needs medical review rather than reassurance alone.

For every sleep, place the baby flat on their back on a firm, clear sleep surface. Do not elevate the cot or use side or front sleeping to treat reflux. Upright holding after a feed is not a replacement for safe sleep positioning.

Some babies need a clinician-directed thickening plan or a specific formula. Do not add extra formula powder, cereal or another thickener to a bottle on your own. Adding extra powder changes the feed’s concentration. The clinician should first consider the feeding pattern and possible conditions, including cow’s milk protein allergy, before choosing treatment.

4. Colds, coughs and influenza

Mucus, gagging and a strong coughing spell can sometimes lead to vomiting. A child may have a runny or blocked nose and cough without a fever. Babies encounter many respiratory viruses as their immune system develops, but a particular number of colds cannot explain an individual episode of vomiting.

Watch breathing and feeding as well as the vomit. A baby who cannot feed comfortably because of congestion or who repeatedly vomits after coughing may need help. Persistent severe coughing, pauses in breathing, blue or grey colour, chest pulling in with breaths or unusual drowsiness require urgent assessment.

Colds and influenza are not interchangeable in severity, and recovery is not guaranteed within a week. Influenza can cause significant illness in young children. Antibiotics are used for appropriate bacterial infections, not for a routine cold, and a new or worsening illness should be assessed on its own merits.

5. Ear infection or an ear-related illness

Ear infections are common in early childhood and can occur alongside nausea or vomiting. Children’s middle-ear drainage pathways differ from adults’, which contributes to their susceptibility. Some ear conditions can also affect balance, but vomiting or dizziness alone does not identify an ear infection.

Possible clues include ear pain, rubbing or pulling an ear, disturbed sleep, irritability, feeding difficulty or reduced hearing. Diarrhea or other symptoms may accompany a wider illness. Ear pulling is also common for other reasons, so an examination may be needed.

Many uncomplicated ear infections improve without antibiotics, but treatment decisions depend on age, symptoms and examination findings. Seek advice for a young baby, significant pain, ear discharge, swelling around or behind the ear, or a child who appears unwell. Hearing changes that persist after an infection also deserve follow-up.

6. Overheating and heat illness

Too much clothing, a hot room, direct sun or a hot vehicle can overwhelm a baby’s ability to regulate temperature. Heat illness may cause vomiting, thirst, irritability, pale or clammy skin and unusual tiredness. A child may not have an infection-related fever, but their body temperature can still rise dangerously.

Move the child to a cooler place, remove unnecessary layers and start gentle cooling. If the child is alert and can swallow safely, offer age-appropriate fluids; a young baby usually needs breast milk or correctly prepared formula and prompt advice if feeding is difficult. Water should not replace a young infant’s milk feeds.

Call emergency services for altered awareness, collapse, a seizure, breathing difficulty or suspected heatstroke. Continue cooling with cool water and fanning while waiting for help. Do not force drinks into a drowsy or unresponsive child. A baby who remains unusually sleepy, floppy or unwell needs urgent care, even if the temperature reading is uncertain.

Never leave a child alone in a vehicle, including during a short stop. Avoid overwrapping and check the baby’s comfort during hot weather rather than assuming that a thick outfit is needed because the womb was warm.

7. Motion sickness during travel

Motion sickness happens when the signals reaching the brain from the eyes and balance system do not agree. Nausea, pallor, sweating, yawning, restlessness or increased saliva may appear before vomiting. It is less typical in children under two, so recurrent vomiting in a baby should not automatically be blamed on the car.

For an older child who is prone to motion sickness, a cool, well-ventilated car, breaks and looking outside instead of at books or screens may help. Avoid a large heavy meal immediately before travel, but do not withhold a baby’s needed feeds while waiting for complete digestion. A familiar nap time may make a journey easier without being a guaranteed prevention method.

Keep the child in the correct car seat with the harness, direction and recline required by its instructions. Do not add unapproved head supports or alter the restraint to reduce movement. Stop safely before taking a child out of the seat to comfort or clean them.

Ask a clinician before using motion-sickness medicine in a child. Symptoms that also occur away from travel, or include headache or changes in walking, vision or hearing, need assessment for another cause.

8. Milk-related conditions are not all the same

Cow’s milk protein allergy, lactose intolerance and galactosemia are different conditions. They should not be grouped together as a single milk intolerance or managed by switching products without advice.

A milk protein allergy is an immune reaction and may cause vomiting with skin, bowel or breathing symptoms. Lactose intolerance concerns digestion of the milk sugar lactose and more often causes diarrhea, gas, bloating or discomfort; it is uncommon as a primary problem in young babies. A lactose-free formula can still contain cow’s milk protein and is not a general treatment for milk allergy.

Classic galactosemia is a rare inherited problem processing galactose, a sugar obtained from lactose in milk. Affected newborns can become seriously ill soon after feeding begins, including with poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, lethargy or infection. Both breast milk and standard milk-based formula can be relevant. It is not an ordinary itchy milk allergy.

Newborn screening may detect galactosemia, depending on the local programme, and an abnormal result requires rapid follow-up. Screening does not justify waiting when a newborn is unwell. Suspected or confirmed classic galactosemia needs urgent specialist care and a suitable feeding plan that restricts galactose and lactose.

Do not stop all nutrition, substitute an ordinary plant drink or select a formula only by looking for the words milk protein. The appropriate formula and longer-term care depend on the diagnosis. Seek immediate help for vomiting with breathing difficulty, collapse or a rapidly developing allergic reaction.

9. Pyloric stenosis

Pyloric stenosis develops when the muscle at the stomach outlet thickens and narrows the passage into the intestine. It usually presents in the early weeks of life, often between two and six weeks, with vomiting that becomes progressively more forceful after feeds. The vomit is usually not green.

A baby may seem hungry again afterwards but still lose fluid and nutrition. Poor weight gain, fewer wet diapers and fewer stools may develop. Visible waves across the abdomen can occur, but they do not have to be present for the condition to be considered.

A baby with repeated projectile vomiting needs urgent assessment. Clinicians may use ultrasound and blood tests, then correct dehydration and disturbed body salts before surgery to relieve the obstruction. This is not a problem to solve by repeatedly changing feeding technique at home.

10. Intussusception

Intussusception occurs when one section of bowel slides into the next, potentially obstructing it and compromising its blood supply. It is most common in infants and toddlers, although it can happen at other ages. Many cases have no clear cause; a recent viral illness does not mean a virus has directly damaged and folded the bowel.

A child may have episodes of severe pain, pull their knees up, become pale or vomit, and appear better between episodes. Unexplained marked lethargy can be an important sign, sometimes without an obvious pain pattern. Blood or mucus in the stool may appear later; do not wait for it or for green vomiting before seeking help.

This needs emergency hospital assessment. Ultrasound is commonly used, and treatment may involve an image-guided air or liquid enema by a specialist team. Surgery is needed in some cases. A parent cannot safely push the bowel back into place by hand, and this is not a home-massage problem.

Recognise dehydration and replace fluids safely

Look for fewer wet diapers or less urine than usual, a dry mouth, sunken eyes, few tears, unusual irritability or sleepiness, and a sunken soft spot in a baby. No single sign proves the degree of dehydration. A change from the child’s usual feeding and urine pattern matters.

Do not wait eight to twelve hours for a wet diaper if a baby is already feeding poorly or looking unwell. The threshold for advice is lower for young babies, and worsening alertness or breathing is an emergency. Contact a clinician promptly when a child cannot keep fluids down.

For a child who is alert, has no emergency signs and can drink, offer small amounts frequently. Continue breastfeeding when tolerated. Keep formula at its usual correct concentration. A clinician or pharmacist can recommend an age-appropriate oral rehydration solution and explain the amount to offer.

Mix rehydration products exactly as directed. Do not use extra powder, large volumes of plain water for a young infant, or fizzy drinks as substitutes. If small drinks repeatedly come back up, seek advice; hospital treatment may be needed when oral fluids are not enough.

Once tolerated, return to ordinary age-appropriate food without forcing it. Do not give anti-vomiting or anti-diarrhea medicines to a young child unless advised. If obstruction, serious illness or another emergency is suspected, obtain urgent help instead of continuing a home hydration trial.

What to tell the clinician and what to expect next

Describe the child’s age, when vomiting began, how often it happens, whether it is forceful, and any green or bloody material. Mention feeds, new foods, diarrhea, pain, cough, travel, heat exposure, possible swallowed medicines or toxins, and the last wet diaper or urine.

Tell the clinician if weight gain has slowed or vomiting has become a recurring pattern. Although many episodes settle, persistent or unexplained vomiting can have causes beyond those described here. Normal temperature does not exclude infection, an abdominal problem or a condition outside the digestive system.

Assessment may be limited to history and examination in a well child, or may involve blood tests, urine testing or imaging when indicated. If you are sent home, ask what improvement to expect and which changes should prompt an earlier return. Trust a clear deterioration in the child’s condition rather than waiting for a fever or a fixed twelve-hour deadline.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pediatric guidance treats vomiting as a symptom with several possible causes. Green vomit, reduced responsiveness and signs of dehydration require particular attention, and vomiting without diarrhea should not automatically be called gastroenteritis.

Independent references cover reflux, infections, heat illness, motion sickness and the less common metabolic or surgical causes. Age, associated symptoms and the child’s overall condition determine the urgency of assessment.

How BeMama can help

Record the episode pattern, feeds and wet diapers, but prioritise how the child looks and responds. Seek help early for a young baby or any deterioration.

When to seek help

Green or bloody vomit, a very painful or swollen abdomen, difficulty waking, breathing trouble or a seriously unwell child requires emergency assessment. A normal temperature is not reassurance on its own.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Vomiting can occur without fever, including in serious illness.
  • Effortless spit-up differs from repeated forceful vomiting; the baby’s wellbeing and growth matter.
  • Keep fluids age-appropriate and formula correctly prepared; seek advice for dehydration or inability to drink.
  • Green vomit, marked lethargy, severe abdominal symptoms or a very unwell child need urgent assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Can a child have a stomach bug without a fever?

Yes. Fever may be absent, and vomiting can precede diarrhea. However, vomiting without diarrhea also has other causes, so a normal temperature should not be used to diagnose a stomach bug or rule out an emergency.

Is curdled milk vomit dangerous?

Milk can look curdled after contact with stomach acid. The texture alone does not show whether an episode is serious. Repeated forceful vomiting, poor feeding, green or bloody material, or an unwell baby needs assessment.

When is green vomit an emergency?

Green vomit can contain bile and indicate a bowel obstruction. A baby or child with green vomiting needs emergency assessment, even without fever. Do not wait for repeated episodes.

Should I add cereal or extra powder to stop reflux?

Do not alter a feed’s concentration or add cereal or thickener on your own. A clinician may prescribe a specific thickening plan for selected babies after assessment. Extra formula powder is not a safe general reflux treatment.

Can a baby with reflux sleep on their side?

No. Put the baby flat on their back on a firm, clear sleep surface. Do not raise the cot or use side or front sleeping as reflux treatment. Upright holding is for an awake caregiver and does not change safe sleep advice.

How long should I wait if my baby has fewer wet diapers?

Do not wait for a fixed interval if the baby is feeding poorly, repeatedly vomiting or looking unwell. Fewer wet diapers can indicate dehydration. Young babies need early advice; difficulty waking or breathing requires emergency care.

Is lactose-free formula suitable for every milk-related problem?

No. It may still contain cow’s milk protein, so it does not generally treat milk protein allergy. Galactosemia is a separate metabolic condition requiring a specialist feeding plan. Ask for a diagnosis before changing formula.

Why does my baby seem hungry after projectile vomiting?

That pattern can occur with pyloric stenosis, particularly in the early weeks, though it is not enough to diagnose it. Repeated forceful vomiting in a baby needs urgent assessment rather than more feeding experiments.

Can intussusception happen without blood in the stool?

Yes. Blood or mucus may appear later or may not be obvious. Recurrent severe pain, pallor, vomiting or unexplained marked lethargy can be clues and need emergency assessment.

Should I give medicine to stop the vomiting?

Use anti-vomiting medicine only with clinical advice appropriate to the child’s age and likely cause. Stopping the vomiting does not prove that the underlying problem is harmless. Hydration and warning signs still need attention.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
